plain: Midjourney generates images from a written description. It's the tool that produces the best aesthetic finish on the market and gives the most control over style, in exchange for a learning curve: writing 'a nice house' isn't enough, you have to learn to describe things the way a photographer or an art director would. It's good for product images, illustration, backgrounds, moodboards, covers, and graphic material. It's not good for anything with written text or logos: that gets added afterward.

account.free: There's no free plan. The entry-level plan ran around $10 a month as of August 2026 and gives a limited number of fast-generation hours; higher plans range from about $30 up to about $120 a month and add unlimited generation in relaxed (slow) mode. Check for yourself at midjourney.com. Two things that matter as much as the price: on basic plans your images are public and show up in the community gallery, and commercial use is tied to your plan and your company's billing. Read this before using an image in client work.
steps: You can now work directly from the web, without going through Discord like you had to at first. If you find a tutorial that starts by installing Discord, it's outdated.
Sign up and pick a plan
With Google or with Discord. You need to enter a card from the start: there's no free version.
Check whether your images will be public

In the settings. On basic plans, everything you generate shows up in the community's public gallery. If you're working for a client on something confidential, you need private mode, which comes with the higher plans.
The box at the top. Start with something specific: an object, a place, a scene. It'll give you back four versions.
Learn the two buttons that matter
Below the four images: U to upscale one of them to full resolution, and V to request variations of the one you liked. Those two cover 90% of your working time.
Along with the model version and the parameters. Without that notebook, a win can't be repeated or tweaked.
account.warning: What you generate on basic plans is public and shows up in the community gallery, including anything you make for a client. If the work is confidential, or the client doesn't want it visible before launch, you need private mode. And check commercial use before invoicing: it depends on your plan and your company's billing.

first: Write a prompt describing what's seen, not what you want to convey: subject, setting, light, framing.
Look at the four versions it gives you and click V on the one closest to what you were after, not the prettiest one.
Repeat the same prompt adding only one lighting detail ('late-day side light') and compare. That's where you understand the power of light.
Try adding --ar 16:9 at the end to change the aspect ratio. It's the parameter you'll use the most.
Save the prompt that worked best to a file, parameters included.
shortcuts: Upscales image 1, 2, 3, or 4 of the four it gave you to full resolution. The 'this one works' button.
Requests four new variations based on that one. The 'you're on the right track, keep going' button.
--ar 16:9 for landscape, --ar 9:16 for vertical mobile, --ar 1:1 for square. The most-used parameter.
--no text, --no hands. Used to remove things that sneak in. Doesn't always obey, but it helps.
How much artistic freedom it takes. Low sticks to your description; high looks prettier and less faithful. If your images come out gorgeous but not what you asked for, lower this.
Locks the randomness so you can repeat a result. Same as with video: it's what turns a win into something reproducible.
You can drag in an image and use it as a starting point or a style reference. It's what gets the result closest to what you have in mind.
Character reference and style reference: keeping the same character or the same style across different images. It's what lets you make a coherent series instead of four loose images.
daily: Describe like a photographer: subject, setting, light, framing, optics. 'Close-up of a ceramic mug on wood, side light from a window, blurred background' works. 'A nice mug' doesn't.
Work iteratively: generate, pick the closest one, request variations, repeat. Rewriting the whole prompt every time is starting from zero over and over.
Always start with --ar. The aspect ratio determines the composition: asking for landscape and then cropping to vertical ruins the framing.
If it comes out pretty but isn't what you asked for, lower --stylize. It's the setting people don't know about and the one that solves that exact complaint.
Don't waste a single attempt on it writing text or drawing a logo. It doesn't know how. That gets added on top with any editor.
Save your good prompts with parameters and seed. It's your real asset: three months from now it's worth more than the images.

templates.name: The prompt structure that works
templates.what: Midjourney responds to ordered visual descriptions, not adjectives. This structure puts things in the order the tool weighs them: what comes first carries the most weight. Works for product, illustration, scenes, and portraits.
templates.how: 1) Fill it in left to right; the important part goes first. 2) Light and framing aren't optional: they're what separates an amateur image from a professional one. 3) Parameters go at the end, after everything else. 4) Generate, pick the closest one, and request variations instead of rewriting everything.
fill: The first thing and the most specific. A specific object, not a category
Where it is and on what. Changes the result enormously
Time, direction, and hardness. The ingredient that stands out the most
Close-up, wide shot, overhead. And the lens if you know it
--ar always. --s if it comes out too loose. --no to remove things
templates.code:
[SPECIFIC SUBJECT], [SETTING], [LIGHT], [FRAMING AND OPTICS],
[STYLE OR FINISH] --ar [RATIO] --s [0-1000]

─── EXAMPLES THAT WORK ────────────────────────────────────

Product:
white athletic sneaker on wet concrete, city street at dawn,
soft side light with long shadows, low ground-level close-up,
product photography, blurred background --ar 4:5 --s 250

Scene:
interior of a neighborhood bakery early in the morning, flour
dust in the air backlit, worn wooden counter, wide shot from
the doorway, documentary photography --ar 16:9 --s 150

Illustration:
flat illustration of a woman working on a laptop in a coffee
shop, three-color palette, simple geometric shapes, no text
--ar 1:1 --s 500 --no text

─── RULES ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Whatever you write first carries the most weight.
2. Concrete nouns, not catalog adjectives.
3. Light, always. It's what changes the result the most.
4. No text or logos: added afterward in an editor.

errors: The text that appears in the image is misspelled

It doesn't know how to write: it draws shapes that resemble letters. Don't waste attempts on this. Generate the image without text (add --no text) and place the text on top with any editor, where it'll also be sharp and the exact right size.
The classic. Three ways out: frame it so they don't appear, have hands hold an object, or switch to a shot with no people. Insisting with the same prompt won't fix it.
It comes out gorgeous but isn't what I asked for

It's the --stylize parameter, which defaults to high and gives it artistic freedom. Lower it (--s 100 or less) and it'll stick much closer to your description, even if it looks less flashy. It's the most common complaint and has an exact fix.
Every image is a different style and I can't get a coherent series
You're generating loose images. Use the style reference (--sref) with an image you like, or lock the seed. To keep the same character across images, use the character reference (--cref).
My images are public and I don't want that

On basic plans everything goes to the community gallery. It's not a glitch or a setting you forgot: private mode comes with the higher plans. If you're working with confidential client material, this needs to be solved before you start.
I've run out of fast hours

The entry plan gives limited fast-generation hours. Once they're gone, either wait for the cycle to reset, switch to relaxed mode if your plan has it, or upgrade. To avoid getting there: settle the framing and light with a few generations and use variations to fine-tune, which stretches further.

prompts.name: Write the prompt for an image I have in my head
prompts.prompt: I want to generate an image in Midjourney and I know what I want, but it comes out in adjectives, so the result is generic. Turn it into a prompt that works. One: ask me at most three questions to pin down the subject, what I'm going to use it for, and where it'll be seen. Two: write me the prompt following the order Midjourney respects: specific subject first, then setting, then light, then framing and optics, then finish, and parameters at the end. Three: choose the parameters yourself and explain each in one line: what aspect ratio and why, what stylize value and why, and whether it's worth excluding something with --no. Four: give me three variants of the same prompt, each changing ONE thing (light, framing, and finish), so I can compare without getting confused. Five: tell me what's likely to go wrong in this specific image and what I should check for when reviewing it. Six: if what I want includes text or a logo, tell me and explain that it gets added afterward in an editor. The image I need is: [DESCRIBE IT AS BEST YOU CAN]. It's for: [WHERE IT WILL BE USED].

prompts.name: Get a series of images that look consistent with each other
prompts.prompt: I need several images that look like they're from the same family, not four loose images that happen to look similar. It's for [WHAT: A WEBSITE, A CAMPAIGN, A CATALOG]. Help me like this. One: ask me how many images I need, what each one shows, and where they'll be seen together. Two: define a common 'style recipe' for me: color palette, type of light, treatment, and framing, written as a chunk of text I can paste identically into every prompt. Three: write out the complete prompt for each image, with that common recipe inside and only the subject changing. Four: tell me how to use the style reference and the seed so consistency doesn't depend on luck, with the exact parameters. Five: tell me what order to generate them in: which one to do first to lock in the style and use as a reference for the others. Six: tell me what to check when viewing them together to know whether they truly look like a series. The images I need are: [LIST].

words: Prompt
The written brief. Here it works to describe what's seen, in order of importance.
U / Upscale
Enlarging one of the four images to full resolution.
V / Variation
Requesting four new versions based on the one you chose. This is how you fine-tune.
--ar
The aspect ratio: 16:9 landscape, 9:16 vertical, 1:1 square. Decided before generating.
--stylize (--s)
How much artistic freedom it takes. High: prettier and less faithful. Low: sticks to what you asked for.
--seed
Locks the randomness. It's what lets you repeat or slightly vary a result you liked.
--sref
Style reference: an image whose look you want the new one to inherit.
--cref
Character reference: keeping the same person across different images.
Public gallery
Where your generations show up on basic plans. Everyone can see it.
Private mode
The option to keep your images from being public. Comes with the higher plans.
matters: Describe like a photographer: subject, setting, light, framing. Light is what most sets a professional image apart from an amateur one, and it's what almost nobody writes.
Work through variations instead of rewriting the whole prompt every time. Picking the closest one and requesting variations is how you get to what you wanted; rewriting is starting from zero.
Know whether your images are public before working for a client. On basic plans they are, and that can be a serious problem with confidential material.
Save good prompts with their parameters and seed. Three months from now, that file is worth more than the images you generated.
ignore: Having it write text or draw your logo. It doesn't know how. That gets added afterward with an editor, and it looks better that way.
The lists of 'magic words' circulating around the internet. What works is a concrete description of what's shown, not piling on adjectives like 'masterpiece, 8K, ultra-detailed'.
The advanced parameters while you're still learning. With --ar and --s you have 90% of the control. Changing five at once means you can't tell what's improving the result.
